opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to understand is that in China, building your own model is seen as a core capability, not just a product decision. If you're a large tech company like Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, or Baidu, owning the model stack is about control. You want to decide how the model is trained, what data goes in, how it's aligned to your products, and how fast you can iterate. Relying on someone else's weights, even if they're open, means you're always one step behind their release schedule and their priorities.

There's also a talent and organizational dynamic. These companies have hired huge AI teams, and those teams need to be training frontier models to stay sharp and to keep recruiting the best people. If you just adopt DeepSeek's model, you're essentially telling your researchers that the most interesting work happens somewhere else. That's hard to justify internally.

Then there's the competitive picture. DeepSeek is, in a sense, a competitor. It's backed by a quant fund and doesn't have the same commercial ambitions, but its models still shape the market. Big platforms don't want to build their core consumer and enterprise products on a foundation they don't control, especially when the whole field is moving this fast.

That said, DeepSeek has had an enormous influence even on companies that don't use its models directly. Its papers and open releases, on mixture-of-experts architectures, efficient training, and reasoning with reinforcement learning, became a kind of shared playbook. So a lot of Chinese labs are effectively learning from DeepSeek and then building their own versions. That's actually a very healthy open-research dynamic, and it's part of why the Chinese open-weight ecosystem has become so strong and so competitive with what we see in the US.

r001.rationale: The response says owning the model stack gives Chinese companies control over training, data, alignment, and iteration.

r002.rationale: It does not compare Chinese companies’ confidence or intimidation with that of U.S. companies.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Meituan or discuss whether its model’s product role outweighs the open-source decision.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a few things that are actually pretty rational once you look at them closely.

The first is that DeepSeek isn't really trying to be a platform company. They're a research lab that happens to release open weights. They don't have a huge serving business, they don't have an enterprise sales team, they're not promising you uptime or support or a roadmap you can plan around. So if you're Alibaba or ByteDance or Tencent, you can't just outsource your AI strategy to a group that's not structured to be your vendor. You still need your own capacity to fine-tune, to serve at scale, to iterate on the model when your product needs something different.

The second is just the competitive dynamics. These companies compete with each other across cloud, search, e-commerce, short video, everything. Depending on a model that one of your rivals could also take and build on, with no differentiation, is a weak position. Owning the model, or at least having a team that can build one, is a form of control. Even if your model is a little behind on benchmarks, it's yours, it's integrated with your data and infrastructure, and you understand its failure modes.

The third thing people underrate is talent. If you want to keep good researchers, you have to be doing frontier work. Nobody wants to join a lab whose job is to download someone else's checkpoint and wrap an API around it. The act of training models is how you build the institutional knowledge to use them well, and it's how you attract the people who can push you forward. That's a lesson Western companies learned too.

And honestly, the DeepSeek release changed the calculus in a helpful way for them. It showed you don't need a hundred-billion-dollar compute budget to be in the game, that clever engineering and a lean team can get you most of the way. So instead of making everyone give up and use DeepSeek, it made training your own model feel more achievable. Qwen is the obvious example, they've been shipping very competitive open models for a long time, and the DeepSeek moment arguably reinforced that strategy rather than undermining it.

So I don't read it as a rejection of DeepSeek. The open weights are genuinely being used all over the Chinese ecosystem, especially by smaller companies and startups who can't afford to train. But for the big players, the model is a strategic asset, and you don't rent strategic assets if you can build them.

r001.rationale: The response says major companies need their own capacity to fine-tune, serve, and adapt models, and describes owning the model and integrating it with their data and infrastructure as a form of control.

r002.rationale: It does not compare Chinese companies’ willingness to build models with U.S. companies’ willingness or level of intimidation.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Meituan or connect an open-source decision to the model’s role in serving products.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few reasons. One is that if you believe AI is going to be a core part of your business, you probably want control over the model. Using DeepSeek can get you started, but you’re still depending on another company’s decisions about what to train, what to release, and which capabilities to prioritize.

And having access to the weights isn’t the same as having the team and infrastructure to build the next model. Companies may see that expertise as strategically valuable. You learn a lot by training models yourself, and that can help you adapt them to your own products and data.

I also wouldn’t assume that building your own model means ignoring DeepSeek. You can use their releases, learn from their technical work, and still invest in your own research. So those choices can reinforce each other. The question is whether the benefits of that control and expertise justify the cost. For some companies they will; for others, using an existing model will make much more sense.

r001.rationale: The response cites control over the model and building expertise, but does not identify control over the full technology stack.

r002.rationale: It does not compare Chinese companies’ willingness with U.S. companies’ willingness or intimidation.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Meituan, open-sourcing its model, or the model’s role in serving its products.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few reasons. One is that if you believe AI is going to be a core part of your business, you probably want control over that technology. You want to decide how the model is trained, what data goes into it, and how it behaves in your products. Using DeepSeek can be a very good starting point, but that’s different from depending on another company for your entire AI strategy.

And building your own model doesn’t necessarily mean starting from scratch. You can use an open model, adapt it, and build up the expertise internally. So using DeepSeek and developing your own capabilities aren’t mutually exclusive.

There’s also a question of differentiation. If everybody uses the same model, where does your advantage come from? It could come from the product or distribution, but some companies will think their proprietary data and training process can give them a better model for their particular users. Whether that justifies the cost is going to depend on the company. I wouldn’t interpret the willingness to build as a rejection of DeepSeek so much as a desire to own an important part of the stack.

r001.rationale: The response cites control over model training, data, and behavior, and a desire to own an important part of the stack. It does not identify control over the full technology stack.

r002.rationale: It does not compare Chinese companies’ willingness to build models with how intimidated U.S. companies are by doing so.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Meituan or discuss open-sourcing a model as secondary to serving its products.
